---
title: "23.10 - Reading Methylation on Each Fish's Own Genome"
format: markdown_github
editor: visual
---

## The question

DNA methylation is a chemical "annotation" layered on top of the DNA sequence — small tags
(methyl groups) attached to certain letters that can turn genes up or down without changing the
letters themselves. It is one of the ways the same genome can behave differently in different
animals, so it is a natural place to look for what distinguishes **lean** and **siscowet** lake
trout.

An earlier step ([14-diff-meth](14-diff-meth.py)) found 302 short stretches of the genome that
looked differently methylated between the ecotypes. All of them were measured against a **single
reference genome** built from a lean-type fish. Now that each ecotype has its *own* assembled
genome, we can ask which of those differences are real.

## What we did

1. **Align to self.** Each fish's PacBio reads (which carry the methylation tags directly) were
   aligned to its own ecotype's genome and methylation was called at every CpG
   ([23.8](23.8-native-meth-pipeline.py)).
2. **A first comparison that came back empty.** Pairing genes across the two genomes by name and
   comparing them site-by-site found almost nothing ([23.9](23.9-native-meth-dmg.py)). That turned
   out to be a power problem: it only used CpG sites read at least ten times in a fish, while most
   fish were sequenced at roughly 8–20×, and its statistical test could not reach significance with
   four fish per group.
3. **Pool the reads.** Adding up every methylation call across a gene's promoter or body rescued
   the low-coverage fish and made about 35,000 genes testable, with a test whose false-positive rate
   we checked by shuffling the fish labels ([23.11](23.11-native-meth-counts.py)). This produced
   over a thousand apparent differences.
4. **Check the yardstick.** Those thousand differences compared lean fish on the lean genome with
   siscowet fish on the siscowet genome, so "ecotype" and "which genome" were tangled together. We
   untangled them by also aligning each ecotype's reads to the *other* ecotype's genome, giving two
   shared yardsticks: on each genome, all eight fish are measured at exactly the same positions
   ([23.12](23.12-native-meth-frame-control.py)).
5. **Place the old differences.** We located each of the 302 reference-based regions on both new
   genomes by sequence alignment and re-tested them on each shared yardstick.

## What we found

- **Most of the thousand "differences" were a yardstick effect.** On a shared genome, the same
  genes look the same in both ecotypes. One example: a promoter read about 65 % methylated in all
  eight fish on the lean genome and about 10 % in all eight fish on the siscowet genome. The
  difference came from the genome, not the fish — the two genomes' versions of that "promoter" are
  different pieces of DNA. Only **63 genes** kept a consistent difference on both yardsticks.
- **Across the genome, gene-level methylation looks the same in lean and siscowet.** On both
  shared genomes the statistics look exactly like there is no difference to find.
- **The old regions split into two groups.**
  - **About half sit in duplicated DNA.** They land in two or more near-identical copies on the
    new genomes, ten times more often than random stretches of the genome. In such places reads
    cannot be placed reliably, so these regions cannot be confirmed or ruled out.
  - **The other half, the ones that land in one clear place, are real.** On the siscowet yardstick,
    where nothing touches the lean reference, 34 of 38 testable regions differ in the same direction
    as originally reported, and 19 are individually significant.
- **No lipid or calcium signal.** The 63 consistent genes include some individually interesting
  ones — a fat-synthesis enzyme (DGAT2-like) more methylated in siscowet, a calcium sensor
  (hippocalcin-like), and the appetite/stress hormone precursor POMC — but as a group they do not
  point to lipid storage or calcium handling.

## Why this matters

This step corrected two earlier readings. The first native pass said the old methylation
differences "did not reproduce", and the pooled analysis briefly suggested over a thousand new
ones. Both were artifacts — one of low coverage, the other of comparing two different genomes. The
fair summary: **ecotype methylation differences are few and localized; the reference-based regions
in unique DNA are genuine; those in duplicated DNA remain open.** It also gives a method lesson for
any two-genome study: compare methylation on a shared genome, in both directions, rather than by
matching gene names across genomes.

## Where to explore

All tables are hosted on gannet under
[analyses/23-native-methylation/](https://gannet.fish.washington.edu/v1_web/owlshell/bu-github/project-lake-trout/analyses/23-native-methylation/):

- The 63 consistent genes and every gene the pooled test flagged, with both yardstick tests —
  `dmf_robust.tsv`
- Every gene feature tested on each shared genome — `dmf_frame_lean.tsv.gz`,
  `dmf_frame_siscowet.tsv.gz`
- The 302 reference regions: where they land on the new genomes and how they test —
  `ref_dmr_native_loci.tsv`, `ref_dmr_frame_tests.tsv`, `ref_dmr_placement_mapq.tsv`
- Plain-text summaries — `native_meth_counts_report.txt`, `native_meth_frame_report.txt`

## What's next

- **Position-level scan on a shared genome.** Gene-sized windows can blur a sharp local
  difference; repeating the original region-finding method on each shared yardstick is the
  natural follow-up.
- **Fold methylation into the evidence model** alongside presence/absence and gene-content lines.
- **Phase 4 — new genes.** A from-scratch gene annotation (BRAKER3) of each ecotype's genome to
  find genes the reference cannot show.

The large intermediate files (alignments and per-site methylation calls) are too big for GitHub
and stay on the lab server.
